## Pick R or Python once {#pick-r-or-python-once}

Every example on this site is written twice: once in **R** and once in **Python**. Both give the same answer. Click a tab to choose. The site remembers your choice on every page, so you only pick once. (The EN, DE and FR links at the top of the page change the language of the text, not of the code.)

Here is a tiny example: five pretend patients' ages, their [mean](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term}, and their [standard deviation](../glossary.qmd#standard-deviation){.term} (SD).

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ages <- c(64, 71, 58, 69, 75)   # five pretend patients' ages

mean_age <- mean(ages)           # the average
sd_age <- sd(ages)               # the standard deviation

mean_age
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 67.4
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sd_age
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 6.580274
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd

ages = pd.Series([64, 71, 58, 69, 75])   # five pretend patients' ages

mean_age = ages.mean()                    # the average
sd_age = ages.std()                       # the standard deviation

print(mean_age)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
67.4
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(sd_age)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
6.580273550544841
```


:::
:::

:::



Both say the mean age is 67.4 years with an SD of 6.6 years.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: the standard deviation trap
Python has two common ways to compute an SD, and they disagree. `pandas` (`ages.std()`) divides by *n − 1*, like R's `sd()`. `numpy` (`np.std(ages)`) divides by *n* unless you write `np.std(ages, ddof=1)`. Medical papers report the *n − 1* version. Whenever the two languages' defaults differ, this site sets them explicitly and explains why in a box like this one.
:::

Behind the scenes, every page checks that the R and Python answers match. If they ever disagree, the site refuses to build, so you can trust that both tabs say the same thing.

## Running the code yourself {#running-the-code-yourself}

1. Open the repository folder in Positron (see [Install & set up](setup.qmd)).
2. Save practice files in the `scratch/` folder, for example `scratch/practice.R` or `scratch/practice.py`. Git ignores everything in `scratch/`, so practice files can never be committed by accident.
3. Copy code with the copy button that appears in the top-right corner of every code block.
4. Run a line with **Cmd+Enter** (Mac) or **Ctrl+Enter** (Windows). Positron sends it to the console.

Data paths such as `data/cohort.csv` are relative to the repository's top folder. Positron starts there when you open the folder, so the paths just work.

## How results are reported {#how-results-are-reported}

Every "How to report it" paragraph on this site follows the same rules, which match what reviewers at journals such as JBJS, *The Bone & Joint Journal* and *CORR* expect.

| What | Report it as | Example |
|------|------|------|
| [Continuous](../glossary.qmd#continuous-variable){.term}, roughly [symmetric](../glossary.qmd#symmetric){.term} | [mean](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term} ([SD](../glossary.qmd#standard-deviation){.term}) | age 67.4 (6.6) years |
| Continuous, [skewed](../glossary.qmd#skewed){.term} | [median](../glossary.qmd#median){.term} ([IQR](../glossary.qmd#iqr){.term}: the interquartile range, from the 25th to the 75th [percentile](../glossary.qmd#percentile){.term}) | length of stay 1 (0 to 2) days |
| [Categories](../glossary.qmd#categorical-variable){.term} | n (%) | 312 (52%) female |
| [p-values](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term} | three decimals; never "p = 0.000" or "p = 1.000" | p = 0.017; p < 0.001; p > 0.999 |
| [Effect estimates](../glossary.qmd#estimate){.term} | with a 95% [confidence interval](../glossary.qmd#confidence-interval){.term} | difference 1.6 kg/m² (95% CI 0.7 to 2.5) |

The examples in the table are illustrations, not results from our data. [Demographics (Table 1)](../foundations/02-demographics.qmd) shows the full [Table 1](../glossary.qmd#table-1){.term} layout.

**Results sentences give the numbers and stop there:** each group's value, the estimate with its 95% CI, and the p-value. Leave out words that interpret them, such as "similar", "higher than", "more often", "improved", "[significant](../glossary.qmd#statistical-significance){.term}", "no clear evidence", or labels like "good" or "moderate". Saying what the numbers mean is the Discussion's job. An illustration:

> KOOS JR at 1 year was a median of 87 points (IQR 76 to 94) in men and 85 (IQR 73 to 94) in women (Hodges-Lehmann difference 1 point, 95% CI −2 to 4; p = 0.432).

The [Hodges-Lehmann difference](../glossary.qmd#hodges-lehmann){.term} in this illustration is the median of all the differences between one man's score and one woman's score. It is not the difference between the two medians, so it needn't equal 87 − 85 = 2 ([page 6](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#mann-whitney) explains it).

Around each Results sentence, this site's text does interpret the numbers, because that's how you learn to read an output. The Results sentence itself is the part to copy into a manuscript.

## Exercises {#exercises}

Each page ends with two to four short exercises on the practice data. They get harder in three steps: run the same analysis on a different [variable](../glossary.qmd#variable){.term}, pick the right test for a short scenario, then write the Results sentence. Solutions are hidden in both languages. Try first, then check.

**Try it:** using the same five ages, find the **[median](../glossary.qmd#median){.term}**.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ages <- c(64, 71, 58, 69, 75)
median(ages)   # the middle value when the ages are sorted
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 69
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd

ages = pd.Series([64, 71, 58, 69, 75])
print(ages.median())   # the middle value when the ages are sorted
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
69.0
```


:::
:::

:::

Both print the median, 69 (Python writes it as `69.0`).

:::
